title: Computing ideal class groups

problem.name: Computing ideal class groups
problem.statement_latex: For a number field $K$, compute invariant factors and represented generators of the finite abelian ideal class group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$. Equivalently, produce an explicit decomposition into cyclic groups together with ideals representing their generators. The class group parametrizes ideal classes and important isogeny group actions. Complexity is measured in quantum gates and classical bit operations on explicit number-field and ideal representations.
problem.statement_text: For a number field $K$, compute invariant factors and represented generators of the finite abelian ideal class group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$. quantum.headline_latex: Polynomial time under GRH, Biasse--Song class-group computation.
quantum.details_latex: The parameters are the number-field degree, logarithmic discriminant and standard encoding lengths. The output gives invariant factors and represented ideal generators. The cost includes finding the relevant $S$-unit relation lattice and classical Smith normal form; GRH bounds the small-prime generating set used by the reduction.
quantum.headline_text: Polynomial time under GRH, Biasse–Song class-group computation.

classical.headline_latex: $L_{|\Delta|}[1/2,O(1)]$ in imaginary quadratic fields, Hafner--McCurley and Buchmann index calculus.
classical.details_latex: The stated bounds use the analytic and smoothness hypotheses of the corresponding relation-collection algorithm. Factor-base relations and integer linear algebra recover a presentation of the same finite abelian class group. For fields of arbitrary degree, the applicable bound varies with degree and discriminant; the imaginary-quadratic family is the explicit matched comparison here.

strength.description_latex: Subexponential to polynomial in the quadratic-field regime, through hidden-lattice Fourier methods.

evidence.description_latex: Partial evidence for separation. The quantum polynomial bound is conditional on GRH, and the classical subexponential algorithms have their stated analytic or smoothness assumptions.

hardware.description_latex: Polynomial logical space supports coherent number-field arithmetic and high-precision Fourier sampling. Cryptographic instances require fault tolerance; concrete workspace and gate counts depend on the field family and arithmetic circuits.
